# Tracks, Groups and Objects

A student joins our lecture ten minutes after it begins. They want the lecturer’s voice and a small video that fits their connection. They do not need the earlier ten minutes, the high-resolution video, or anyone else’s captions.

To make that choice possible, the publisher has to give its data some structure. MoQ uses **tracks** to separate things a viewer can request, **groups** to organize portions of a track, and **objects** to identify individual pieces of data. We will build that structure from the viewer’s request down to one encoded picture.

## A track is something you subscribe to

Our lecture has an audio track, a low-resolution video track, and a high-resolution video track. A **track** is a named sequence of groups. Subscribing to `video-low` asks for that sequence; it does not also request `video-high`.

Tracks belong to a **namespace**, which lets the application organize related names. For this lecture, we use the namespace `lectures / session-7`. Together, the namespace and track name identify the full track.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Selecting tracks from a lecture
  accDescr: The lecture namespace contains audio, video-low, and video-high tracks. The example viewer subscribes to audio and video-low.
  L["Namespace: lectures / session-7"] --> A["Track: audio"]
  L --> V["Track: video-low"]
  L --> H["Track: video-high"]
  A --> S["Student receives audio and low-resolution video"]
  V --> S
```

These readable labels are examples. On the wire, MOQT represents namespace components and track names as byte sequences. Both ends must agree on those bytes; writing the same-looking path in a user interface is not enough. See [track naming in draft-21 §2.4.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-2.4.1).

## Groups create places to join

Choosing a video track leaves another question: where should the student start?

Many compressed pictures describe changes from earlier pictures. Receiving one of these **predicted frames** without its reference pictures is like receiving “move it two pixels to the left” without knowing what “it” is. A **keyframe** provides a picture from which decoding can restart.

For our video format, the publisher begins each group with a keyframe, then puts the frames that depend on it in the same group. The student can start with a recent group instead of reconstructing the entire lecture. The player also needs the codec configuration, which the media format supplies separately.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  accTitle: Two independently decodable video groups
  accDescr: Group 41 starts with its own keyframe and dependent frames. Group 42 starts with a new keyframe and has no picture dependency on group 41 in this example.
  subgraph G41["Group 41"]
    direction TB
    A["Object 0: keyframe"] --> B["Object 1: predicted frame"]
    B --> C["Object 2: predicted frame"]
  end
  subgraph G42["Group 42"]
    direction TB
    D["Object 0: new keyframe"] --> E["Object 1: predicted frame"]
    E --> F["Object 2: predicted frame"]
  end
```

Each arrow runs from a reference picture to a picture that needs it. These are decoding dependencies, not network packets. A viewer who has missed group 41 can still use group 42. This is why [MOQT recommends independently useful groups](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-2.3). A group boundary alone cannot make a picture decodable: the publisher must put a suitable picture there.

Group IDs order groups within the track. Group 42 does not mean “42 seconds,” and groups need not have equal duration. The media format carries timing information for playback.

## An object is a named piece of data

Inside each group are **objects**. Each object has an ID and a payload: the bytes being delivered. Our example puts one encoded picture in each object. Other media formats can divide their data differently.

We can now give a complete address for one picture:

| Part of the identity | Example | What it selects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Track namespace | `lectures / session-7` | This lecture |
| Track name | `video-low` | Its low-resolution video |
| Group ID | `42` | One group in that track |
| Object ID | `1` | One piece of data in that group |

The identity applies within an agreed **scope**: the set of servers that treat a full track name as the same track. An unrelated service can use the same labels for different content. Within our lecture service’s scope, however, that complete identity must consistently refer to the same payload. See [objects (§2.1)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-2.1) and [scope (§2.5)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-2.5).

This property is called **immutability**. Once published, an object’s payload does not change. If Alice and Bob request the same object, a relay can serve the same stored bytes to both. A corrected payload needs a new identity; otherwise the relay would have no way to know which version the name means.

## Subgroups decide what shares a stream

We have described what the content is. We also need to decide which objects should travel together.

For subscription delivery, MOQT can divide a group into **subgroups**, each carried on a subgroup stream. Within a subgroup, objects are ordered by object ID. This lets the publisher separate work that benefits from separate transport streams.

For example, a layered video codec might produce a base layer that gives a usable picture and an enhancement layer that adds detail. Putting them in separate subgroups lets a scheduler favor the base layer when capacity is scarce. The enhancement still depends on the base; a separate stream does not remove that media dependency.

A subgroup organizes delivery; its ID is not an extra component of the object address in the table above. Objects delivered as datagrams do not belong to subgroups, and fetched objects have their own stream representation. These distinctions are defined in [draft-21 §2.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-2.2).

## Restarting is a naming problem too

Suppose the lecturer’s publisher crashes. When it restarts, it reuses `video-low`, group 42, object 1 for a new picture. A relay still has the old picture stored under that address. It cannot safely treat both as the same immutable object.

One solution is to give the restarted publication a fresh namespace, such as `lectures / session-8`. Another is to preserve a non-conflicting sequence of group IDs. The application must choose a strategy that keeps old and new identities distinct throughout its scope.

The same naming rules that make caching useful make this restart decision necessary. In the next chapter, we will follow a request for one of these named tracks from the student to the publisher.

## A vocabulary translation

When working with the moq-lite implementation, you will encounter **broadcast** for a named collection of tracks and **frame** for the payload unit corresponding to an object. moq-lite omits MOQT subgroups and uses a simpler group-per-stream model. Keep that distinction in mind when moving between [its documentation](https://doc.moq.dev/concept/moq-lite) and the IETF specification.
